doc.title: Greg Thomas interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, October 11, 2014

title: Booking concerts: fit, audience and themes
summary: Asked whether race is a booking consideration, Thomas says fit matters, and describes G&J themes such as 'Cutting Up' and 'Jazz Plus'.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Well getting back to when you produce concerts and so forth. Are you conscious of the people that you book in a whole season or for a particular event? Because we both sort of agree that there’s no such thing as race, but I can’t say this question without it. Are you conscious, like gee I have booked almost all white players this season, or I have booked almost all black players this season. You know when I get the musicians for this Fallcoming jazz concert, that’s been going on for 23 years and there’s been many years where all the musicians were white, partly because they played in a style that our founder Milt Fillius liked.
I don’t know if I have a question here. But I wonder if —

If race, so-called, is a consideration either retrospectively or prospectively? Not race per se, because I’ve hired men, women, black, white, you know Latino, Asian — and they’ve been mixtures in the band, which is always great. But you do have to take a look at fit. When I say fit, fit could be stylistic fit, fit could be generational, because who’s your audience? As a writer it’s like you’ve got to be aware of who your audience is so when you’re booking/producing, who’s your audience? Now your audience in your case is varied. And a jazz audience is certainly hard to define, but when we book in Harlem for example, you know you’re usually talking about boomers and older. You’ve got some Gen Xers yeah. You usually don’t have a lot of young people, and the young people you do have, either they were introduced to the music by their parents and the event is just something they can do that’s fun. Or they are musicians, they’ve studied music. You know a lot of times those are the things that when we see young people. But, you know, what’s your theme? See one of the things we do for G&J is we have different themes that we use to hang the events on. So instead of just presenting such-and-such a group led by such-and-such a person (which we’ve done also) you have a certain theme that you’re fitting groups in for a series. So we had something called “Cutting Up,” which was based on the cutting content. So you have the leaders on the same instrument, with the rhythm section and they’re playing tunes together, and they’re trading fours and trading eights and that kind of thing. It’s really fun but to use the whole competition angle it’s kind of a marketing tool of sorts. And we’ve had, oh man, we’ve had several of those concerts, very successful. In fact one of them ended up on Dr. Henry Louis Gates’ of the African Americans Many Rivers to Cross, his Peabody and Emmy-award winning PBS series for example. We have one that’s called “Jazz Plus” that allows us to have jazz at the center but it’s jazz plus rock, jazz plus Latin, jazz plus rock, jazz plus classical. So that’s another theme. You also have — we had one that was a singer series, that you give it a certain title. So the question is more for us, how does a particular group fit underneath the theme that we’re presenting for the audience we’re presenting to. So those are the real main
considerations certainly because — certainly not race. But you do want to have the right fit for what you’re trying to present.
Yeah. And personalities and all that.
